youtube_title: Why doesn't half power look half as bright? Dimmer curves explained
linkedin:
Why doesn't a light at half power look half as bright?

Because the eye does not measure light in straight amounts. Our sense of brightness works by comparison, so equal steps in light output do not look like equal steps. A light cut to half its output still looks roughly three quarters as bright. To look half as bright, it has to come down to somewhere around a fifth of its output. The standard model of perceived lightness used in colour science gives about 18 per cent for a mid grey, which is why that figure turns up in photography as well.

If a fader controlled output in a straight line, most of the visible change would be crowded into the bottom of its travel, and the top half would seem to do very little. So many fixtures and consoles offer dimmer curves. A square law curve, for example, makes the output the square of the fader position: half way on the fader gives a quarter of the light, which looks close to half.

What that means for an event:

1. Fades look smoother. With a suitable curve, a slow fade looks even from start to finish instead of seeming to happen all at the end.

2. Match the curve across the rig. Fixtures set to different curves will not track each other during a fade, even on the same fader.

3. Low levels need care. Very dim settings are where LED fixtures differ most, so smooth fades at the bottom are worth checking during programming.

The honest limit: the figures are averages. Perception also depends on the surroundings, the colour of the light and how adapted the eyes are, and curves vary between manufacturers.
